## Eight common assumptions, negated

1. **More convs always give more accuracy, independent of the other edges.** If false, a conv edit's gain shrinks or reverses when a parallel conv already feeds the same node (saturation, scale mismatch at the sum).
2. **A skip is always a free, helpful shortcut.** If false, a skip hurts when the conditioning edge already supplies an unmodified or parameter-free path, because it duplicates that path.
3. **Pooling is a mild regularizer that is neutral to slightly negative.** If false, pooling interacts with its neighbours. It over-smooths when the neighbour is also a pool and helps when it follows a conv.
4. **Deeper chains are better.** If false, a conv downstream of a pool or skip is wasted, while a conv downstream of a conv has the highest value.
5. **Removing an edge costs the same wherever it sits.** If false, the cost depends on whether another path reaches the node.
6. **Gradient flow matters only on the edited edge.** If false, a direct skip into node 3 matters more when the chains behind it are deep.
7. **1x1 and 3x3 convs are interchangeable up to capacity.** If false, a 1x1 conv gains from a spatially mixing neighbour, and 3x3 gains from a channel-mixing or skip neighbour (multi-scale complementarity).
8. **Interactions seen on 32x32 CIFAR carry over to 16x16 ImageNet16-120.** If false, the over-smoothing and depth effects would flip sign. I chose hypotheses whose mechanism should hold on all three datasets.

I made no literature retrieval calls. Main effects here come from background knowledge: conv3x3 > conv1x1 > skip > pool > none, with skip helping trainability. Only two hypotheses (1 and 2) argue "equivalent capacity exists elsewhere". No hypothesis conditions on the edited edge, and none uses a condition that disconnects the edited edge.
